prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, long-term disability, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but profit margin is decreasing.
prompt.question: What should Vitality do about its declining profit margin?

clarifying_info.q: How does Vitality sell its products?
clarifying_info.a: All policies are sold through Vitality's field sales agents, who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium — defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other compensation mechanisms for agents beyond base commission?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. In addition to standard commission, short-term priorities are communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity and pay a bonus on top of standard commission.

clarifying_info.q: What are Vitality's major cost categories?
How large is Vitality's sales force?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has over 10,000 field sales agents.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has a few competitors who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the market leader. Competition is not the primary focus of this case.
This is a mature market. Agent turnover is typically very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Key Results and Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key operating metrics and major cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in $000s)

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process and Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A diagram of Vitality's selling process steps (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Keep accounts active, Upsell active accounts, Produce results / Premium $, Reactivating dormant accounts) with the number of sales contests targeted at each leverage point broken out by year (2008, 2009, 2010)

exhibits.title: Snapshot of Sweeps Week Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart plotting weekly premium (as a ratio to the 2008-2010 average weekly premium) for weeks 1-27 (January through June) for years 2008, 2009, and 2010. Two weeks in 2010 are annotated as 'Sweeps Week' contests (weeks 4 and 20).

data.y_axis: Ratio to Average Weekly Premium (2008-2010), scaled 0%-200%

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs. Confirm revenue trend (growing at ~10%/yr) vs. cost trend (identify which cost line is anomalous).
Decompose costs: G&A, Sales, Advertising — identify that Sales costs spike abnormally from 2009 to 2010.
Investigate the sales cost driver: understand how agents are compensated (base commission + sales contests) and whether contest structure changed.
Examine the sales process value chain (Exhibit 2) and contest mix shift: 2008/2009 vs. 2010.
Evaluate whether the incremental contest spending generated incremental revenue (ROI of contests).
Recommend action: eliminate or redesign contests that duplicate the main commission incentive or cause gaming behavior.

questions.prompt: Calculate the year-over-year growth rates of premium, G&A, Sales costs, and Advertising from 2008-2009 and 2009-2010. What stands out?
questions.guidance: All line items except Sales costs grow at approximately 10% per year. Sales costs also grow at ~10% from 2008 to 2009, but grow at ~45% from 2009 to 2010, while premium growth remains at 10%. Profit margins decline from 9.50% to 9.40% to 8.50%, accelerating in the 2009-2010 period. Strong candidates quickly flag the 2010 Sales cost anomaly.

steps: Conclusion: Sales costs grew 4.5x faster than revenue in 2010
math.answer: Sales costs grew ~45% from 2009 to 2010 while premium grew only 10%, causing significant margin compression. All other cost lines grew roughly in line with revenue.

questions.prompt: Looking at the sales process and contest mix (Exhibit 2), what changed in 2010 versus prior years?
questions.guidance: In 2008 and 2009 the contest mix was identical: 2 contests on acquiring new accounts, 4 on keeping accounts active, 1 on upselling, and 2 on producing premium results. In 2010 the mix shifted substantially: contests on keeping accounts active dropped from 4 to 0, contests on acquiring new accounts doubled from 2 to 4, and contests on producing total premium doubled from 2 to 4. This means Vitality shifted its 2010 incentive focus toward total premium volume and new account acquisition, away from retaining and growing existing accounts. Strong candidates note this mirrors a marketing mix rebalancing.

questions.prompt: One of the new 2010 premium-focused contests was called 'Sweeps Week.' Vitality launched two Sweeps Week contests paying an extra 10% bonus on all premium booked in weeks that were traditionally low volume. What does Exhibit 3 reveal about its effectiveness?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 shows that Sweeps Week (weeks 4 and 20 in 2010) generated very high premium volume in those specific weeks — appearing as sharp spikes well above 100% of average. However, the weeks immediately before and after each Sweeps Week are notably below the average, forming a 'valley.' This strongly suggests agents were gaming the system by shifting enrollment timing (pulling forward or pushing back sales by up to a week) to book premium during the bonus window. The net incremental premium from Sweeps Week is therefore likely minimal or zero — it merely redistributed when sales were recorded. The contest's focus on total premium was also duplicative with the main commission structure, adding cost without adding value.

math.setup: Extra contest cost = 10% bonus on premium booked in Sweeps Weeks. If agents merely shift timing rather than generate new sales, incremental premium = ~0, so contest cost is pure incremental expense.
steps: Visually confirm: 2010 weeks 4 and 20 have ratios well above 100% (high spikes)
Visually confirm: surrounding weeks in 2010 have ratios well below 2008/2009 baselines (valleys)
Pattern = timing redistribution, not incremental volume
If Sweeps Week premium ≈ borrowed from adjacent weeks, net new premium from the contest ≈ 0
Contest cost = 10% × (premium booked in those two weeks) = paid out with no corresponding revenue benefit
math.answer: Sweeps Week incentivized agents to game enrollment timing. Net incremental premium generated was approximately zero. The 10% bonus paid during those weeks was therefore pure incremental sales cost with no offsetting revenue benefit, directly depressing profit margin.

questions.prompt: What is the likely profit margin impact of the new 2010 contests focused on acquiring new accounts (even without detailed data)?
questions.guidance: Acquiring a new customer is considerably more costly than retaining or up-selling an existing policyholder. By shifting 4 contests toward new account acquisition (up from 2) and eliminating all 4 contests focused on keeping accounts active, Vitality's sales force was redirected away from lower-cost revenue activities. Even without exact numbers, strong candidates should articulate that new-customer acquisition costs more per dollar of premium generated, so a mix shift toward new accounts structurally worsens the cost-to-revenue ratio. This further explains the margin compression in 2010.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond eliminating Sweeps Week, what types of sales contests or incentive structures could Vitality use to drive profitable growth without encouraging gaming or duplicating the existing commission structure?

categories.name: Retention and relationship deepening
ideas: Contests rewarding agents for keeping existing policyholders enrolled (reducing lapse rates)
Bonuses tied to policyholder tenure milestones
Team contests rewarding the lowest churn rate per territory

categories.name: Targeted up-sell / cross-sell
ideas: Contests for adding additional coverage types to existing policyholders
Bonuses for successfully upselling to higher benefit tiers
Activity-based contests rewarding the number of up-sell conversations held

categories.name: New account quality (not just quantity)
ideas: Contests rewarding new accounts above a minimum size threshold
Bonuses tied to new account activation rates (not just signed contracts)
Contests for acquiring accounts in specific high-value industries or geographies

categories.name: Agent development and productivity
ideas: Contests rewarding newer agents for hitting first-year production milestones
Peer mentoring incentives to reduce turnover and onboarding cost
Training completion bonuses tied to measurable skill assessments

categories.name: Contest design improvements to prevent gaming
ideas: Use rolling 4-week windows instead of fixed single weeks to average out gaming
Cap the bonus at a defined volume ceiling per agent to reduce artificial spikes
Set minimum performance floors in surrounding weeks for the bonus to be earned

recommendation: Eliminate the Sweeps Week contest for 2011. The contest generated no net incremental premium — it only redistributed when agents booked existing sales — while paying a 10% bonus that materially increased the sales cost base.
Repurpose the Sweeps Week budget toward contests that target activities not already covered by the main commission structure, such as policyholder retention or targeted up-sell programs.

Review and potentially reduce the number of new-account-focused contests added in 2010, as a pure new-account push increases per-unit acquisition cost and structurally worsens margins; reinstate some retention-focused contests (which were eliminated in 2010).
risks: Removing Sweeps Week may be unpopular with the sales force, which perceived it as a favored program, potentially affecting morale or short-term agent retention.

It is unclear whether the four new-account contests added in 2010 reflect a deliberate strategic shift to grow market share; eliminating them without understanding the strategic intent could undermine a valid growth initiative — further data is needed before acting on these.
High agent turnover (outside of the recessionary period) means any contest restructuring must be communicated clearly to avoid misinterpretation and accelerated departures.
next_steps: Quantify the net premium attributable to Sweeps Week (compare Sweeps Week premium to depressed adjacent weeks) to confirm the gaming hypothesis with data.
Survey or interview sales agents and sales managers to understand perceptions of the 2010 contest mix and surface any unintended consequences.
Model the incremental cost per new account vs. retained/upsold account to size the margin impact of the new-account contest shift before deciding whether to reduce it.
Design a 2011 contest calendar aligned to activities that are additive to — not duplicative of — the standard commission structure, with anti-gaming mechanics built in.
